newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire says U.S. backs Rwanda war effort.
newsitem.headline: Zaire says U.S. backs Rwanda war effort.

text.p: Zaire accused the United States on Monday of supplying Rwanda with equipment used against the Zairean army which has lost ground in fighting in the east.

Government spokesman Boguo Makeli told Reuters that assault speed boats donated by Washington to the Rwandan government were used by Rwandan army troops in attacks on the eastern Zaire town of Goma last week.

"We also captured certain weapons from the enemy which carry 'Made in USA' and 'Made in Australia' trade marks," Boguo said. "Certain services have informed us that these weapons are being supplied to Rwanda via neighbouring Uganda."
The speedboats used by the Rwandan army are based in Lake Kivu and can carry up to 25 men at high speed across the lake.
The Zairean army has been handed a series of defeats in its two border provinces of North and South Kivu since fighting between it and ethnic Tutsi rebels exploded about two weeks ago.
The army has lost control of three major towns around Lake Kivu -- Uvira, Bukavu and Goma -- forcing international aid workers to withdraw from there.

Zaire accuses Rwanda, whose army and government are dominated by Tutsis, of invading its territory. It also links Burundi and Uganda to the fighting. Independent sources say Rwandan troops have been involved on the ground inside Zaire.

Rwanda has admitted sending troops across the border into Zaire but maintains fighting in eastern Zaire is between the Zairean army and Banyamulenge Tutsi rebels resisting Zaire's attempts to expel them.
Rwanda accuses Zaire of sheltering armed Rwandan Hutu hardliners who massacred up to a million minority Tutsis or their sympathisers in 1994 and then fled into Zaire.
Zaire charges that Tutsis who went on to win civil war in Rwanda in 1994 are trying to annex the east as a buffer zone against a possible Hutu invasion from its territory.
Camps in eastern Zaire sheltering more than one million Hutu refugees have emptied during the two weeks of fighting.
Boguo went on to accuse the United States of double standards in its regional policy.
"Zaire is astounded that the U.S. authorises governments which took power by force to destabilise a neighbour which is bringing in democratic reform," the minister said.
"If the United States makes exceptional cases as it has with Rwanda there will be no more democracy in the region," he said.
Zaire has said it will not take part in peace talks on the fighting until Rwandan troops withdraw from its territory.
President Daniel arap Moi of Kenya is expected to meet leaders of Tanzania, Uganda, Zambia, Rwanda, Ethiopia and Cameroon in Nairobi on Tuesday.

Moi on Sunday urged South African President Nelson Mandela to suspend all arms sales to Rwanda until Rwandan troops withdrew from eastern Zaire, Moi's office said, quoting a telephone discussion between the two leaders.
Mandela has said he is examining South Africa's arms sale contracts with Rwanda in the light of the Zaire conflict.
